passage:
Salma typed the message on her phone in the office stairwell, deleted it twice, then sent it: "Something is wrong with the vendor payments. Please look into it." She left out her name, dates, amounts, everything, because she was scared of being traced.

Two days later, Kishore, the investigator, read it at his desk in the compliance wing. He looked for a date, a file name, any figure he could check, and found none. "We can't verify anything from this," he told his manager, and closed the file.

Nothing happened. The payments carried on. Salma refreshed her email every hour for a week, sleeping badly, wondering whether she had done anything at all except worry.

qa.q: Where did Salma type her message?
qa.a: In the office stairwell, on her phone.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as she waited after sending the message?
qa.a: Salma felt anxious and uncertain, shown by refreshing her email every hour, sleeping badly and wondering whether she had done anything.

qa.q: What could Salma do differently, and why?
qa.a: Salma could collect dates, amounts and file references first and send a factual report through a protected channel, because investigators can only act on something they can check.

qa.q: How does Kishore see a message with no details?
qa.a: Kishore has nothing to test, so a report that might be real must be closed, even though it may hide a genuine problem.

grounding: A person sends a vague anonymous message with no dates or documents, investigators cannot verify it, and the person stays anxious.

passage:
'They closed it,' Chaitanya said, dropping his phone on the table at the dhaba.
Hrithik looked up from his paratha. 'Closed what?'
'The anonymous tip I sent the ethics hotline. About the site manager.' He read the reply aloud. '"Insufficient information to proceed. No further action."'
'What did you send?'
'That the site manager is doing something wrong with the cement orders and someone should look into it.'
'That's it?'
'I didn't want them to know it was me.'
'No dates? No order numbers?'
'I was scared. I just wanted it out of my head.' Chaitanya rubbed his forehead. 'It isn't out of my head. It's worse. Now it's been "looked into", nothing happened, and I still know what I saw.'
Hrithik pushed his plate aside. 'Do you still have the order slips?'
'Photos of three of them. With dates.'
'Then next time, send those. You can still stay anonymous. Just not empty.'

qa.q: What did the ethics hotline reply?
qa.a: 'Insufficient information to proceed. No further action.'

qa.q: How does Chaitanya feel after the tip is closed?
qa.a: More anxious than before, still carrying what he saw and frustrated that nothing happened.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya include in a new report?
qa.a: The dates and order numbers from the photographed slips, so investigators can check them while he stays anonymous.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see the tip Chaitanya sent?
qa.a: Hrithik sees it was too vague to act on, and points out gently that anonymous does not have to mean empty.

grounding: Shows a person sending a vague anonymous tip with no dates or documents, which is dismissed while the worry remains.

passage:
I'm Tarun. Last year at the call centre, I saw a team leader marking absent agents as present so their shifts were paid. It happened on at least six days that I remember. I was scared of being known as the one who told.
So one night I made a new email address and wrote to the company's ethics inbox: 'Attendance fraud is happening in the second-floor team. Please check.' No names, no dates, no screenshots. I hit send and felt like I'd done something brave.
Two weeks later a reply came to that address: 'Thank you. We were unable to identify the matter from the information provided. If you have further details, please share them.' That was all.
Parveen, who had seen the same thing, asked if I'd written down the dates. I hadn't. By then the attendance screens had been overwritten.
I still think about it. I wanted to do the right thing with no risk at all. What I did was the least risky thing, and it did nothing.

qa.q: What did Tarun's anonymous email say?
qa.a: 'Attendance fraud is happening in the second-floor team. Please check.'

qa.q: How did Tarun feel right after sending the email, and later?
qa.a: Brave at first, then frustrated and uneasy when the reply showed it could not be acted on.

qa.q: What could Tarun have included to make the tip useful?
qa.a: The dates, the team leader's role and screenshots of the attendance entries, still sent anonymously if needed.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel about how it turned out?
qa.a: Disappointed and a bit frustrated, having seen the same thing and hoped the report would work.

grounding: Shows a person sending a vague anonymous message with no dates or evidence, which investigators cannot verify, while the worry stays.
